title: Inside Sadhguru's Inner Engineering: What the 22-Hour Program Teaches About Yoga and the Mind
excerpt: The program, which combines online learning with an in-person transmission of Shambhavi Mahamudra Kriya, has drawn millions worldwide — and a growing following among Indian diaspora professionals.
body:
• Inner Engineering is a 22-hour program combining online self-paced learning with a live weekend transmission of Shambhavi Mahamudra Kriya, a 21-minute daily yogic practice
  • Founded by Sadhguru through the Isha Foundation, the program operates across more than 300 centers worldwide with over 11 million volunteers
  • Sadhguru's New York Times bestselling book of the same name presents yoga as a sophisticated system of self-empowerment beyond physical exercise
  • The program has gained particular traction among Indian diaspora professionals in the U.S., where Sadhguru recently keynoted the IIT2026 Global Conference in Long Beach, California

Beyond the Yoga Mat

When most people in the West think of yoga, they picture a studio class focused on physical postures. But Sadhguru, the Indian mystic and founder of the Isha Foundation, has spent decades arguing that what passes for yoga in gyms and wellness studios is just one of eight branches of a far deeper system of human transformation. His flagship program, Inner Engineering, is designed to take participants into that deeper territory.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=PzWsUrTKEWg

The program is structured as a 22-hour journey spread across seven steps. The first six steps — totaling about 9.5 hours — can be completed online at one's own pace and cover practical tools for daily living, yogic practices for physical balance and rejuvenation, and guided processes aimed at expanding self-awareness. The seventh and final step, a 12.5-hour weekend intensive offered live, involves the transmission of Shambhavi Mahamudra Kriya, a 21-minute practice that combines elements of meditation, breathwork, and inner focus.

The program does not require any prior experience with yoga or meditation, and Sadhguru has been explicit that it is not tied to any belief system. "As a guru, I have no doctrine to teach, no philosophy to impart, no belief to propagate," he has written. "The only solution for all the ills that plague humanity is self-transformation."

From Southern India to Silicon Valley

Sadhguru — born Jagadish Vasudev in Mysore, Karnataka — describes his own path as an unlikely one: a motorcycle-riding young man with an unusual affinity for the natural world who experienced a moment of profound awakening on Chamundi Hill at age 25. That experience led him to establish the Isha Foundation in 1992, which has since grown into a sprawling non-profit with operations in more than 300 centers and a volunteer base exceeding 11 million people.

His 2016 book, "Inner Engineering: A Yogi's Guide to Joy," became a New York Times bestseller and was named one of the ten best books of the year by Spirituality & Health. It distilled the program's core philosophy into an accessible narrative, blending personal memoir with practical instruction. Sir Ken Robinson praised it as "a loving invitation to live our best lives."

"If we want humanity to enjoy the fruits of science and technology rather than using them to destroy the entire planet, the most important thing that needs to be done right now is raising human consciousness."

— Sadhguru, IIT2026 Global Conference

Named one of India's 50 most influential people, Sadhguru has spoken at the United Nations, the World Economic Forum, and major global conferences. In April 2026, he delivered the opening keynote at the IIT2026 Global Conference in Long Beach, California, where he spoke to a predominantly diaspora audience about the balance between technological advancement and inner well-being.

Why It Resonates With the Diaspora

Inner Engineering has found a particularly receptive audience among Indian professionals abroad. In the United States, the Isha Foundation offers programs in major cities with significant Indian diaspora populations, and the program's hybrid online-plus-weekend format fits the schedules of busy professionals who may not have time for extended residential retreats.

The appeal goes beyond cultural familiarity. Many participants describe the program as filling a gap that neither traditional therapy nor fitness-focused yoga addresses — the need for daily practices that systematically work on mental clarity, emotional balance, and what Sadhguru calls "inner engineering" of one's own experience. In a professional culture where burnout, anxiety, and the pressure to perform are constant, the 21-minute daily kriya practice has become a practical anchor for thousands.

The program is offered at a reduced fee in many markets, reflecting the Foundation's stated goal of making wellbeing tools accessible. It is currently available in 10 languages, including English, Hindi, Spanish, French, German, and Mandarin.

What Critics and Science Say

Inner Engineering is not without its skeptics. Some critics question whether a program rooted in mystical traditions can deliver measurable health outcomes, while others have raised concerns about the commercialization of practices that were historically transmitted freely in Indian ashram traditions.

However, a growing body of research has examined the physiological effects of practices like Shambhavi Mahamudra Kriya. Studies have reported improvements in markers of cardiovascular health, reduced cortisol levels, and enhanced emotional well-being among regular practitioners, though researchers note that larger, more rigorous trials are still needed.

For the millions who have completed the program, the proof tends to be more personal than clinical. The daily 21-minute practice — a commitment Sadhguru describes as "non-negotiable" for those who are serious about transformation — becomes either a lifelong anchor or an abandoned experiment. As Sadhguru himself puts it: "This is not about teaching you new things. This is about helping you unlearn what is not working."
